title: Reaction kinetics
objectives: Explain and use the terms rate of reaction, frequency of collisions, effective and non-effective collisions
Explain qualitatively, in terms of collision frequency, the effect of concentration and pressure on the rate of reaction
Use experimental data to calculate the rate of a reaction
Define activation energy and sketch and explain the Boltzmann distribution, including the effect of temperature on it
Explain qualitatively the effect of temperature on rate in terms of the Boltzmann distribution and collision frequency
Explain the terms catalysis and catalyst, including homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts, and explain catalysis using reaction pathway diagrams and the Boltzmann distribution
prior: Activation energy and reaction pathway diagrams (Chapter 5)
why: Chemistry is not only about whether a reaction can happen, but how fast. Kinetics explains why food lasts longer in a fridge, why catalytic converters work and why industry chooses the temperatures it does. Boltzmann distribution questions are on nearly every Paper 1, and rate graphs and explanations appear regularly in Paper 2 and in the practical papers.
intro: Particles must collide, with enough energy and in the right orientation, to react. This chapter uses collision theory and the Boltzmann distribution to explain the effects of concentration, pressure, temperature and catalysts on the rate of reaction, and shows how rates are measured from experimental data.

sections.title: Rate of reaction and collision theory

blocks.h: The change in amount or concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Units: for example mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, or cm³ s⁻¹ for a gas volume.

Reactions happen when particles collide. An effective (successful) collision has energy ≥ the activation energy and the correct orientation. Most collisions are non-effective: the particles just bounce apart.

head: change
effect on collisions
effect on rate
rows: more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions
same particles in a smaller volume → more frequent collisions
more surface exposed → more frequent collisions

blocks.wrong: Higher concentration makes more particles have enough energy to react.
blocks.right: Concentration and pressure change only the frequency of collisions. The proportion with enough energy is the same, because the temperature is the same.

items: Collect a gas in a gas syringe and record volume against time.
Record the loss in mass as a gas escapes.
Follow a colour change with a colorimeter (use a calibration curve to turn absorbance into concentration).
Take samples, quench them and titrate.

blocks.h: On a graph of amount against time, the rate is the gradient. It is steepest at the start (highest concentration) and falls to zero when a reactant runs out. The average rate over an interval = change ÷ time taken.

blocks.name: rateexp
blocks.title: Rate experiment
blocks.h: Change the acid concentration, temperature, chip size and the volume of acid. Compare your experiment (blue) with the original (grey): which changes make it faster, and which change the final volume?

blocks.q: 50.0 cm³ of H₂O₂ decomposes (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂) and 120 cm³ of O₂ (room conditions) is collected in 60 s. Calculate the average rate of decomposition of H₂O₂ in mol s⁻¹ and in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
blocks.err: Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio between H₂O₂ and O₂.

blocks.h: In a gas the molecules have a range of energies. The Boltzmann distribution shows how many molecules have each energy.

items: The curve starts at the origin: no molecules have zero energy.
It rises to a peak (the most probable energy), then falls.
It approaches the energy axis but never touches it: there is no maximum energy.
The area under the curve = the total number of molecules.
The area to the right of E<sub>a</sub> = the number of molecules that have enough energy to react.

blocks.name: boltz
blocks.title: Boltzmann distribution lab
blocks.h: Raise the temperature and watch the curve flatten and shift right while the shaded area beyond E<sub>a</sub> grows. Then add a catalyst at constant temperature and compare.

items: The peak moves to the right (higher energy) and becomes lower; the curve becomes broader.
The total area stays the same.
A much larger proportion of molecules now have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>.
Molecules also move faster, so they collide slightly more often.

blocks.h: So more collisions per second are successful and the rate increases. The main reason is the larger proportion of molecules with E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>; a 10 °C rise often roughly doubles the rate.

blocks.alt: Two Boltzmann curves from the origin; the higher-temperature curve has a lower peak further right and lies above the other at high energy. Activation energy line marked.
blocks.cap: At a higher temperature (T₂) the peak is lower and further right, and more molecules lie beyond E<sub>a</sub>.

When you sketch a second curve: start at the origin, make the peak lower and further right, cross the first curve once, keep it above the first curve at high energy, and do not let it touch the axis.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

head: homogeneous
heterogeneous
rows: catalyst in the same phase as the reactants
catalyst in a different phase from the reactants
H⁺ in esterification; Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ in S₂O₈²⁻ + I⁻; NO₂ in oxidising atmospheric SO₂
Fe in the Haber process; V₂O₅ in the Contact process; Ni in hydrogenation; Pt/Rh/Pd in catalytic converters

blocks.h: On a Boltzmann distribution, a catalyst moves the Ea line to the left. The curve does not change (same temperature), but a larger area now lies beyond Ea, so more collisions are successful per second.

On a reaction pathway diagram the catalysed hump is lower. Reactant and product levels, and so ΔH, are unchanged. Both forward and reverse barriers are lowered by the same amount, which is why a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.

blocks.wrong: A catalyst gives the particles more energy.
blocks.right: The particles have the same energies. The catalyst lowers the energy needed.

blocks.h: Reactions in more than one step
A profile with two humps shows two steps with an intermediate in the dip. The step with the higher barrier is the slower one and controls the overall rate.

blocks.q: Why are catalysts so important in industry?
blocks.a: They allow reactions to run at a useful rate at lower temperatures, saving energy and cost (and often improving yield for exothermic equilibria). They are not used up, and they can make the process more selective.

items: A catalyst changes ΔH for a reaction.
Reactant and product energies are unchanged.
V₂O₅ is a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction too.
The same alternative route is used in both directions.

summary: Rate = change in amount or concentration per unit time; on a graph it is the gradient.
Effective collisions need energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub> and the correct orientation.
Higher concentration, pressure or surface area → more frequent collisions → faster. The proportion with E ≥ E<sub>a</sub> does not change.
Boltzmann distribution: starts at the origin, has a peak, never meets the energy axis; area = number of molecules.
Higher temperature: peak lower and further right; same area; many more molecules with E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>; collisions slightly more frequent.
Catalyst: alternative route with lower E<sub>a</sub>; not used up; ΔH and the Boltzmann curve unchanged.
Homogeneous catalyst: same phase as reactants. Heterogeneous: different phase.
A catalyst lowers forward and reverse E<sub>a</sub> equally, so the equilibrium position is unchanged.
In a multi-step reaction the step with the highest barrier is the slowest.

Energy ≥ activation energy and correct orientation

flash.q: Why does higher pressure increase the rate of a gas reaction?
flash.a: More particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react

flash.q: What does the area under a Boltzmann curve represent?
Why does the Boltzmann curve never touch the energy axis?
flash.a: There is no maximum energy a molecule can have

flash.q: Effect of higher temperature on the Boltzmann peak?
flash.a: Lower and moved to higher energy

flash.q: Main reason higher temperature increases rate?
flash.a: A greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>
Increases rate without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with lower E<sub>a</sub>
A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants

flash.q: Does a catalyst change the Boltzmann distribution?
flash.a: No: it moves E<sub>a</sub> to the left

flash.q: In a two-step profile, which step is slower?
flash.a: The one with the higher energy barrier

practice.q: Explain, using collision theory, why powdered zinc reacts faster with acid than zinc granules of the same mass.
practice.a: Powder has a larger surface area, so more zinc atoms are exposed and collisions with acid particles are more frequent.

practice.q: 0.30 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess acid in 50 s. Calculate the average rate in mol s⁻¹ of Mg used.
Sketch the Boltzmann distribution and label E<sub>a</sub>. Show the effect of a catalyst.
practice.a: Curve from the origin, peak, long tail not touching the axis; E<sub>a</sub> line to the right of the peak; catalysed E<sub>a</sub> line further left; more area beyond it. The curve is unchanged.

practice.q: Explain why a 10 °C increase in temperature can double the rate even though the average speed of the molecules increases only slightly.
practice.a: The proportion of molecules with energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (in the tail of the distribution) increases greatly, so many more collisions are successful.

practice.q: Classify each catalyst as homogeneous or heterogeneous: (a) Ni in hydrogenation of alkenes (b) H⁺(aq) in ester hydrolysis (c) Pt in a catalytic converter.
A catalyst lowers E<sub>a</sub> of a reaction from 120 to 70 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹. Give E<sub>a</sub> of the reverse reaction with and without the catalyst.
practice.a: without: 160 kJ mol⁻¹; with: 110 kJ mol⁻¹

assessment.q: Units of rate when concentration is measured?
Increasing the concentration of a solution increases rate because…

o: touches the energy axis at high energy
has a total area equal to the number of molecules

assessment.q: Raising the temperature makes the peak of the Boltzmann curve…
assessment.why: Broader, lower curve shifted to higher energy.

assessment.q: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ gives 48 cm³ O₂ (room conditions) in 20 s. Average rate of H₂O₂ use?
Why does the rate decrease during a reaction?
assessment.why: Fewer collisions per second as reactants are used.

assessment.q: Which change does NOT increase the proportion of molecules with E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>?
On a gas-volume against time graph, the reaction has finished when…
o: the line passes through the origin
assessment.why: No more gas is produced: gradient zero.

assessment_s.q:
Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
(a) Describe how the rate could be followed using a gas syringe. [2]
(b) Explain, in terms of collisions, the effect of using the same mass of smaller chips. [2]
(c) The experiment is repeated at a higher temperature. Use a Boltzmann distribution to explain the change in rate. [3]
assessment_s.a:
(a) connect a gas syringe to the sealed flask and record the volume of CO₂ at regular time intervals
(b) larger surface area exposed; more frequent collisions → faster
(c) curve lower and further right (same area); more molecules have E ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per unit time

assessment_s.q:
In the Haber process an iron catalyst is used.
(a) Is the catalyst homogeneous or heterogeneous? Explain. [1]
(b) Sketch a reaction pathway diagram with and without the catalyst for this exothermic reaction. [2]
(c) Explain why the catalyst does not change the equilibrium yield. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) heterogeneous: solid catalyst, gaseous reactants
(b) products below reactants; two humps from the same reactant level: catalysed hump lower; ΔH arrow unchanged
(c) it lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor

pp.skill: Collision explanation of the effect of concentration
pp.mis: Saying the particles move faster
pp.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of an acid increase the rate of its reaction with marble chips, at constant temperature?
opts: More particles have energy greater than the activation energy.
There are more acid particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent.
pp.exp: Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so collisions happen more often. The energy of the particles (and so the fraction that can react) is unchanged at constant temperature.

pp.skill: Effective and non-effective collisions when concentration increases
pp.mis: Thinking only the effective collisions become more frequent
pp.stem: In a mixture of SO₂ and O₂, some collisions lead to reaction and some do not. More SO₂ is added at constant temperature and volume. How do the frequencies of effective and non-effective collisions change?
pp.exp: All collisions become more frequent. The fraction with enough energy (and correct orientation) does not change at constant temperature, so both effective and non-effective collisions increase.

pp.skill: Average rates from gas-volume data
pp.mis: Using cumulative volume instead of the change
pp.stem: Magnesium reacts with an excess of dilute acid. The total volume of hydrogen is recorded. P is the average rate in the first 20 s; Q is the average rate in the last 20 s. What is P − Q?

pp.skill: Average rate in mol min⁻¹ from a gas volume
pp.mis: Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio of H₂O₂ to O₂
pp.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). In 2.0 minutes, 240 cm³ of oxygen is collected at room conditions. What is the average rate of decomposition of H₂O₂ in mol min⁻¹?

pp.skill: Average rate as a change in concentration per second
pp.mis: Leaving the answer per minute or in moles
pp.stem: 100 cm³ of 0.40 mol dm⁻³ H₂O₂ decomposes with a catalyst. 96 cm³ of oxygen (room conditions) forms in 80 s. What is the average rate of decrease of [H₂O₂]?
pp.exp: n(O₂) = 0.0040 mol; n(H₂O₂) = 0.0080 mol in 0.100 dm³ → Δc = 0.080 mol dm⁻³. Rate = 0.080/80 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

pp.skill: Average rate in mol s⁻¹
pp.mis: Using minutes instead of seconds
pp.stem: 25.0 cm³ of H₂O₂ decomposes with a catalyst. 216 cm³ of oxygen (room conditions) is produced in 3.00 minutes. What is the average rate of decomposition of H₂O₂?

pp.skill: Concentration from the total volume of gas produced
pp.mis: Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio
pp.stem: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous H₂O₂ decomposes completely to give 450 cm³ of O₂ at room conditions. What was the concentration of the H₂O₂?

pp.skill: Using a pressure change to find the extent of reaction
pp.mis: Forgetting that the number of gas moles changes
pp.stem: 88.0 g of N₂O (2.00 mol) is in a sealed vessel at pressure P. With a catalyst it decomposes: 2N₂O(g) → 2N₂(g) + O₂(g). Later, at the same temperature, the pressure is 1.20P. What mass of O₂ is present?
pp.exp: If y mol O₂ forms, 2y mol N₂O is used and 2y mol N₂ forms: total = 2.00 + y. 2.00 + y = 1.20 × 2.00 = 2.40, so y = 0.40 mol O₂ = 12.8 g.

pp.skill: Combining two changes that cancel in rate
pp.mis: Choosing a change that alters the amount of product
pp.stem: Experiment 1: magnesium ribbon with an excess of dilute HCl. Experiment 2: a higher temperature and one other change. Both give the same total volume of H₂ in the same time. What was the other change?
opts: the acid was diluted, but still in excess
a greater mass of magnesium was used
pp.exp: Higher temperature speeds the reaction up; a lower acid concentration slows it down, so they can cancel. Mg is limiting, so the volume of H₂ is unchanged. B and C would make it even faster; D gives more gas.

pp.skill: Matching a change to a volume–time graph
pp.mis: Changing the limiting reactant
pp.stem: Zinc granules react with an excess of hydrochloric acid. In experiment 2 one change is made: the graph rises more steeply but levels off at the same final volume of H₂. What was the change?
opts: the same mass of zinc was used as powder
pp.exp: Powder has a larger surface area, so more frequent collisions: faster. The amount of zinc (the limiting reactant) is the same, so the final volume is the same.

pp.skill: A change that slows a reaction without changing the yield
pp.mis: Thinking a change of catalyst amount changes the yield
pp.stem: 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ H₂O₂ decomposes with MnO₂ as catalyst (curve X). A new curve Y rises less steeply but reaches the same final volume of O₂. Which change gives curve Y?
pp.exp: Adding water lowers the concentration (slower) but keeps the same amount of H₂O₂ (same final volume). More catalyst or higher temperature would be faster; more H₂O₂ gives more O₂.

pp.skill: Following a reaction with a colorimeter
pp.mis: Thinking absorbance is the concentration
pp.stem: The reaction between bromine and methanoic acid is followed with a colorimeter; the orange colour of Br₂(aq) fades. Solutions of known [Br₂] are measured first to make a calibration curve. Why is the calibration curve needed?
opts: to measure the rate directly from absorbance
to convert each absorbance reading into a concentration of Br₂
to check that the temperature is constant
pp.exp: A colorimeter gives absorbance. The calibration curve (absorbance against known concentration) is used to read off [Br₂] at each time, so a concentration–time graph can be drawn.

pp.skill: Interpreting the Boltzmann distribution
pp.mis: Thinking the area is energy
pp.stem: On a Boltzmann distribution curve, what does the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy represent?
opts: the number of molecules with energy greater than or equal to E<sub>a</sub>
the average energy of the molecules
pp.exp: The total area under the curve is the total number of molecules. The area beyond E<sub>a</sub> is the number of molecules that have enough energy to react.

pp.skill: Effect of lowering temperature on the Boltzmann distribution
pp.mis: Thinking the peak gets lower when cooler
pp.stem: The temperature of a gas is decreased. How does its Boltzmann distribution change?
opts: peak lower; more molecules have energy > E<sub>a</sub>
peak higher; more molecules have energy > E<sub>a</sub>
peak lower; fewer molecules have energy > E<sub>a</sub>
peak higher; fewer molecules have energy > E<sub>a</sub>
pp.exp: Cooler: the peak moves to lower energy and gets taller (same total area). Fewer molecules lie beyond E<sub>a</sub>.

pp.skill: What changes the height of the Boltzmann peak
pp.mis: Thinking pressure changes the shape
pp.stem: Which change makes the peak of the Boltzmann distribution lower and moves it to higher energy?
opts: increasing the pressure at constant temperature
decreasing the temperature at constant pressure
increasing the temperature at constant pressure
pp.exp: Only temperature changes the shape: hotter → flatter, broader curve with the peak at higher energy. Pressure and catalysts do not change the distribution.

pp.skill: Number of molecules with energy exactly E<sub>a</sub> at a new temperature
pp.mis: Assuming the whole curve rises when heated
pp.stem: On a Boltzmann curve, E<sub>a</sub> lies well to the right of the peak. The temperature is raised. What happens to the number of molecules whose energy equals E<sub>a</sub> (the height of the curve at E<sub>a</sub>)?
pp.exp: At a higher temperature the curve spreads to higher energies, so it is higher in the tail region where E<sub>a</sub> lies (even though the peak itself is lower).

pp.skill: Identifying distributions at different temperatures
pp.mis: Matching the taller curve to the higher temperature
pp.stem: Curve X is a Boltzmann distribution. Curve Y has a lower, broader peak at higher energy. Curve Z has a taller, narrower peak at lower energy. Which statement is correct?
opts: Y is at a higher temperature than X.
Z is at a higher temperature than X.
Y has a higher activation energy than X.
All three curves have different total areas.
pp.exp: Higher temperature flattens the curve and moves the peak to higher energy (Y). Z is cooler. E<sub>a</sub> does not depend on temperature, and the area (total number of molecules) is the same.

pp.skill: Activation energy does not change with temperature
pp.mis: Moving E<sub>a</sub> with the curve
pp.stem: The temperature of a reacting gas mixture is increased. What happens to the activation energy?
pp.exp: E<sub>a</sub> is a property of the reaction pathway. Heating changes the distribution of molecular energies, not E<sub>a</sub>. Only a catalyst (a new pathway) changes E<sub>a</sub>.

pp.skill: Full explanation of the temperature effect on rate
pp.mis: Thinking E<sub>a</sub> falls when heated
pp.stem: A gas mixture reacts faster at a higher temperature. Which row of statements is correct?
opts: more molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>: true; E<sub>a</sub> unchanged: true; more successful collisions per second: true
more molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>: true; E<sub>a</sub> unchanged: false; more successful collisions per second: true
more molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>: false; E<sub>a</sub> unchanged: true; more successful collisions per second: true
more molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>: true; E<sub>a</sub> unchanged: true; more successful collisions per second: false
pp.exp: A higher temperature gives more molecules with E ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (the main reason) and slightly more frequent collisions, so more successful collisions per second. E<sub>a</sub> does not change.

pp.skill: Which changes increase the proportion of molecules able to react
pp.mis: Thinking concentration changes the energy distribution
pp.stem:
Three changes are listed.
1 raising the temperature
2 adding a catalyst
3 increasing the concentration
Which increase the proportion of molecules with enough energy to react?
pp.exp: Temperature shifts the distribution to higher energies; a catalyst lowers E<sub>a</sub>. Both increase the fraction beyond E<sub>a</sub>. Concentration increases collision frequency but not the fraction.

pp.skill: Combining temperature and E<sub>a</sub> to compare rates
pp.mis: Considering only one factor
pp.stem: T₂ is higher than T₁, and E<sub>a</sub>(1) is lower than E<sub>a</sub>(2). Which combination gives the slowest rate?
pp.exp: Lowest temperature and highest activation energy: the smallest fraction of molecules beyond E<sub>a</sub>.

pp.skill: Effect of temperature on a profile and a concentration–time graph
pp.mis: Thinking heating lowers E<sub>a</sub>
pp.stem: A reaction goes to completion. Which describes the effect of raising the temperature on its energy profile and on its graph of [reactant] against time?
opts: profile: E<sub>a</sub> lower; graph: falls faster to the same final value
profile: unchanged; graph: falls faster to the same final value
profile: unchanged; graph: falls faster to a lower final value
profile: E<sub>a</sub> higher; graph: falls more slowly
pp.exp: Temperature does not change the pathway, so the profile (E<sub>a</sub> and ΔH) is the same. The reaction is faster, so [reactant] falls more steeply, but it still goes to completion (to zero).

pp.skill: Effect of a catalyst on the Boltzmann distribution
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst changes the curve
pp.stem: An iron catalyst is used in the Haber process. Which describes its effect on the Boltzmann distribution and on the activation energy?
pp.exp: A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower E<sub>a</sub>. The temperature, and so the distribution of energies, is unchanged.

pp.skill: What a catalyst does at the molecular level
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst gives the molecules more energy
pp.stem: A catalyst is added to a slow gas-phase decomposition. Which statement is correct?
opts: The peak of the Boltzmann curve moves to the right.
A greater number of molecules now have enough energy to react.
The kinetic energy of the molecules increases.
The activation energy line moves to the right.
pp.exp: E<sub>a</sub> moves to the left (lower), so more of the existing molecules have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>. The distribution itself and the molecules’ energies are unchanged.

pp.skill: What stays the same when a catalyst is added
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst changes ΔH
pp.stem: At the same temperature, which is the same for a catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction?
opts: the Boltzmann distribution of the reactant molecules
pp.exp: The distribution depends only on temperature. The catalyst changes the pathway, lowering E<sub>a</sub> and increasing the rate. (ΔH is also the same.)

pp.skill: Explaining how a catalyst increases rate
pp.mis: Saying a catalyst increases collision frequency
pp.stem: A catalyst is added to a slow reaction between two solutions at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
opts: It increases the average energy of the particles.
It changes the distribution of particle energies.
It increases the total number of collisions per second.
It allows more of the collisions per second to be successful.
pp.exp: With a lower E<sub>a</sub>, a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy, so more successful collisions happen per second. Particle energies and collision frequency are unchanged.

pp.skill: Combining temperature and catalyst on a Boltzmann diagram
pp.mis: Looking only at temperature or only at the catalyst
pp.stem: A gas mixture can react with or without a catalyst. In which case is the number of molecules with enough energy to react greatest?
pp.exp: The higher temperature puts more molecules in the high-energy tail, and the catalyst lowers the energy needed. Both effects add up.

pp.skill: Heterogeneous catalysis and the reverse reaction
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst only lowers the forward E<sub>a</sub>
pp.stem:
Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process. Two statements are made.
1 Iron is a heterogeneous catalyst.
2 Iron lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction as well as the forward reaction.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: Solid iron with gaseous reactants: different phases, so heterogeneous. The new pathway lowers the barrier in both directions, which is why the position of equilibrium is unchanged.

pp.skill: Catalyst and reacting ratio in the Contact process
pp.mis: Mixing up the Haber and Contact catalysts
pp.stem: In the Contact process, which catalyst is used and in what mole ratio do SO₂ and O₂ react?
pp.exp: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with vanadium(V) oxide. (Iron is used in the Haber process, N₂ : H₂ = 1 : 3.)

pp.skill: Reverse activation energy with a catalyst
pp.mis: Forgetting that ΔH is unchanged by a catalyst
pp.stem: A reaction has E<sub>a</sub> = 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the forward E<sub>a</sub> by 25%. What is E<sub>a</sub> for the reverse reaction with the catalyst?
pp.exp: Catalysed forward E<sub>a</sub> = 60. ΔH is unchanged (−30), so the reverse barrier = 60 + 30 = 90 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: Activation energies and collisions at equilibrium
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst lowers only one barrier
pp.stem:
A ⇌ B is endothermic in the forward direction and happens in a single step. Three statements are made.
1 Ea(forward) is greater than Ea(reverse).
2 At equilibrium, successful collisions happen at the same rate in both directions.
3 A catalyst lowers only the forward activation energy.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: 1: E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) = E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − ΔH, smaller for a positive ΔH. 2: equal rates at equilibrium. 3 is false: both barriers fall by the same amount.

pp.skill: Reading a two-step reaction profile
pp.mis: Judging step speed by product energy rather than barrier height
pp.stem: A reaction profile has two humps. The first barrier is 90 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants. The intermediate is 40 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants, and the second barrier is 20 kJ mol⁻¹ above the intermediate. The products are 35 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants. Which row is correct?
opts: first step slower than second; overall exothermic
first step slower than second; overall endothermic
first step faster than second; overall exothermic
first step faster than second; overall endothermic
pp.exp: The first barrier (90) is much higher than the second (20 from the intermediate), so the first step is slower. Products are below reactants: exothermic overall.

pp.skill: Describing a two-step endothermic profile
pp.mis: Mixing up which step is fast
pp.stem: Which description fits an endothermic reaction that happens in two steps, where the second step is faster than the first?
opts: products above reactants; first barrier higher than the second barrier (measured from the intermediate)
products below reactants; first barrier higher than the second
products above reactants; second barrier higher than the first
products below reactants; only one barrier
pp.exp: Endothermic: products above reactants. The faster step has the smaller barrier, so the second hump (from the intermediate) is smaller than the first.

pp.skill: Activation energy and the Boltzmann explanation of catalysis
pp.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen to form ethane: C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).

parts.q: Name a catalyst for this reaction and state whether it is homogeneous or heterogeneous.
ms: nickel (or Pt/Pd); heterogeneous (solid catalyst, gaseous reactants)
the minimum energy colliding particles need to react

parts.q: Use a Boltzmann distribution to explain how the catalyst increases the rate.
ms: the catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower E<sub>a</sub> (E<sub>a</sub> line moves left on the same curve)
so a greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>; more successful collisions per unit time

pp.skill: Rates from a concentration–time graph and identifying the limiting reagent
pp.stem:
4.00 g of powdered CaCO₃ is added to 100 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid at constant temperature.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
[HCl] / mol dm⁻³ at time / s: 0 s 1.00; 100 s 0.62; 200 s 0.42; 300 s 0.30; 400 s 0.24; 500 s 0.21; 600 s 0.20; 700 s 0.20

parts.q: Calculate the average rate of change of [HCl] between 0–100 s and between 400–500 s. Include units.
Identify the limiting reagent. Explain your answer.
ms: CaCO₃: HCl is still present (0.20 mol dm⁻³) when the reaction stops

parts.q: Explain why the rate decreases with time.
ms: [HCl] falls, so there are fewer collisions per unit time

parts.q: Calculate the volume of CO₂ (room conditions) produced when all the CaCO₃ reacts, and show that this agrees with the final [HCl].
Suggest why measuring the volume of CO₂ gives a slightly low value for the amount of reaction.
ms: CO₂ is slightly soluble in water, so some stays dissolved

pp.skill: Explaining the effect of temperature using the Boltzmann distribution
pp.stem: A gas X(g) decomposes slowly at temperature T₁.

parts.q: Explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the rate of reaction.
ms: particles have more (kinetic) energy, so more have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>
so there are more successful collisions per unit time

parts.q: Describe how the Boltzmann distribution at a higher temperature T₂ differs from that at T₁.
ms: starts at the origin; peak lower and at a higher energy (moved right)
curve is above the T₁ curve at high energies (in the tail) and the area under both curves is the same
